title: Private DR Game Day #1 — notes + timeline (lost control plane DB scenario)
content:
Doc purpose
- Capture an honest timeline from DR game day #1 (what happened, what we did, what broke, what was unclear).
- Feed action items into ENG-4882 (follow-ups) and docs updates.

Game day details
- Date: 2025-11-07 (Fri)
- Scenario: Control plane Postgres data loss / corruption (simulate “lost primary DB volume”)
- Drill type: In-place restore (same cluster) using latest “known good” snapshot + WAL/PITR where available
- Environment: Private (VPC) staging cluster, k8s 1.29, Postgres in-cluster (statefulset + pvc)
- Backup target: S3 (private endpoint) + SSE-KMS
- Expected RPO/RTO (target for this drill)
  - RPO target: <= 30 min (WAL archiving) OR <= 24h if PITR not configured (we attempted PITR)
  - RTO target: 90 min to API “healthy” (basic smoke tests pass)

Participants / roles (in-room)
- Rafael Mendes (SRE lead): incident commander for drill, timekeeper, evidence capture
- Miles Thornton (Reliability architect): scenario design + success criteria
- Ethan Park (Eng lead, control plane hooks): maintenance mode behavior + sequencing questions
- Diego Santos (Platform eng): cluster-level/K8s ops
- Connor O’Brien (Release eng): versioning + “what ships” questions
- Allison Grant (Observability): dashboards/alerts checks
- Sahana Iyer (CI/validation): notes on testability + how to automate restore drill
- Markus Klein (Solutions lead): “would a customer operator understand this?” perspective
- Fatima Noor (Solutions, on-prem): notes on air-gapped deltas (we didn’t run air-gapped today)

Pre-drill setup (completed before start)
- Confirmed scheduled backups are present in bucket (last 3 days).
- Pulled runbooks into a shared window:
  - Runbook: Private restore in-place
  - Runbook: Backup create + verify
  - SRE troubleshooting: backup failures (for reference)
- Opened dashboards:
  - Backup/restore overview dashboard (job success + duration)
  - Control plane service health (API, scheduler, config service)

Timeline (timestamps are real time, PT)

09:02 — Kickoff
- Rafael: reviewed targets (RTO 90m, RPO 30m best effort), reminder that this is “operator-led,” eng only assists when stuck.
- Miles: restated scenario: “DB volume is gone; recover from backups; app should block writes during restore.”

09:07 — Confirm last successful backup and artifact
- Allison opened dashboard: last backup success = 2025-11-07 08:00.
- Markus asked: “Which backup is ‘known good’?” Confusion: dashboard shows last success, but runbook references “latest known good” label in the manifest.

Commands / checks
- kubectl -n redwood-private get cronjob
- kubectl -n redwood-private get job -l app=rw-private-backup
- aws s3 ls s3://rw-private-dr-backups/<cluster-id>/ --recursive | tail

Note: The S3 path convention wasn’t in the runbook; we inferred it from installer config.

09:14 — Verify backup artifact (first confusion)
- Attempted to run verify using local workstation context (wrong kubeconfig).
- Diego: switched to bastion shell.

Commands
- rw-private-dr backup verify --cluster <cluster-name> --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z
- rw-private-dr backup verify --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z

Outcome
- Verify passed checksums on bundle.
- Verify output did not explicitly print encryption mode / KMS key id (we had to look at bucket properties separately). Markus flagged this for enterprise expectations.

09:23 — Inject failure (simulate DB loss)
- Miles: “Pretend the DB disk is unrecoverable.” We deleted the DB PVC to force a recreate.

Commands
- kubectl -n redwood-private scale deploy rw-control-plane-api --replicas=0
- kubectl -n redwood-private scale deploy rw-control-plane-scheduler --replicas=0
- kubectl -n redwood-private delete pvc data-rw-postgres-0
- kubectl -n redwood-private delete pod rw-postgres-0

Observations
- There was debate whether to scale down API first or enable maintenance mode first.
- Ethan: maintenance mode is preferred to stop writes cleanly (if API is still up).
- Runbook order wasn’t explicit (it said “enter maintenance mode” but didn’t clarify whether API should remain running for that call).

09:31 — Enter maintenance mode
- Ethan suggested using the CLI helper instead of direct DB toggles.

Commands
- rw-private-dr restore plan --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z
- rw-private-dr maintenance enable --reason "DR restore drill"  (note: command name not in runbook; we found it in installer README)

Outcome
- Maintenance mode enabled; API started returning 503 on write endpoints with a helpful message (good).
- Confusion: error message referenced “restore in progress” even before restore started (wording nit).

09:38 — Restore attempt #1 (blocked by object storage permissions)
- Restore execution failed early with AccessDenied when trying to read from S3.
- This was the big “unplanned” snag.

Error snippet (redacted)
- AccessDenied: User: arn:aws:sts::<acct>:assumed-role/rw-private-backup-role/... is not authorized to perform: s3:GetObject on resource: arn:aws:s3:::rw-private-dr-backups/<cluster-id>/...

Where we lost time
- We initially assumed the bucket policy was unchanged. It was.
- Root cause ended up being a mismatch between the restore job’s serviceAccount IAM role and the backup job’s role.
- The Helm chart values set backup SA role annotation, but restore job was using default SA.

Commands / investigation
- kubectl -n redwood-private get sa | grep -E "backup|restore"
- kubectl -n redwood-private get job rw-private-restore -o yaml | grep serviceAccountName -n
- kubectl -n redwood-private describe job rw-private-restore

We found
- serviceAccountName: default
- backup CronJob was using serviceAccountName: rw-private-backup

Fix/workaround (for drill)
- Patched restore job to use backup SA.

Commands
- kubectl -n redwood-private patch job rw-private-restore -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"serviceAccountName":"rw-private-backup"}}}}'
- Deleted and re-created restore job (since patch didn’t apply to running pod cleanly).

Time impact
- ~22 minutes lost.

09:59 — Restore attempt #2 (DB sequencing and readiness)
- Restore started; DB pod came up fresh (empty).
- Confusion: runbook referenced “restore DB then bring up control plane” but didn’t state when to unscale API components.

Commands (approx)
- rw-private-dr restore execute --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z --mode in-place
- kubectl -n redwood-private logs job/rw-private-restore -f

Notes
- Restore logs were useful but not structured; hard to quickly find “current step”.
- Allison suggested we emit step-level events for dashboards (“restore_phase=fetch_bundle”, “restore_phase=db_restore”, etc.).

10:14 — PITR attempt (WAL replay)
- We attempted PITR to 08:55.
- We were not confident whether WAL archiving was fully configured in this environment.

Commands (approx; ran inside postgres container)
- kubectl -n redwood-private exec -it rw-postgres-0 -- bash
- ls -lah /var/lib/postgresql/data
- (restore helper invoked by CLI; we did not manually run pg_restore in this drill)

Outcome
- PITR step reported success, but we did not have an easy “verify recovery target time” check in the runbook.
- Michael Nguyen (not present) later Slack’d suggested query: select pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); to validate. Add to runbook.

10:27 — Bring control plane back up
- We scaled API + scheduler back to 1 replica each.

Commands
- kubectl -n redwood-private scale deploy rw-control-plane-api --replicas=1
- kubectl -n redwood-private scale deploy rw-control-plane-scheduler --replicas=1
- kubectl -n redwood-private rollout status deploy/rw-control-plane-api

10:35 — Smoke tests (first pass failed)
- Smoke test step (from rw-private-dr) failed on /v1/models listing (500).
- API logs showed config/policy service failing to connect to DB (migration lock contention).

Commands
- rw-private-dr restore validate --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml
- kubectl -n redwood-private logs deploy/rw-control-plane-api --tail=200
- kubectl -n redwood-private get pods

Confusion / doc gap
- Runbook says “if validate fails, do not exit maintenance mode,” but didn’t explain what counts as “critical” vs “warning.”
- The validate tool just returned non-zero with a list; we debated if it was safe to proceed.

10:46 — Resolve migration/lock contention
- Diego restarted policy/config pods.

Commands
- kubectl -n redwood-private rollout restart deploy/rw-config-service
- kubectl -n redwood-private rollout restart deploy/rw-policy-service

Note
- We should avoid “restart until it works” being the implied solution. Either fix sequencing, add readiness gates, or document expected transient errors.

10:58 — Smoke tests (second pass success)
- /healthz ok
- /v1/models ok
- /v1/chat/completions blocked writes while maintenance was still enabled (expected)

Commands
- curl -k https://<private-api>/healthz
- curl -k https://<private-api>/v1/models

11:04 — Exit maintenance mode + final checks
- Ethan disabled maintenance.

Commands
- rw-private-dr maintenance disable

Checks
- Chat write endpoint accepted request.
- Confirmed dashboards updated “restore drill” annotation manually.

11:13 — Stop clock
- RTO achieved: ~1h 50m from kickoff to “service healthy” (missed 90m target).
- Biggest time sinks: IAM/serviceAccount mismatch (22m) + ambiguity on sequencing (maintenance vs scale down) + validate failure interpretation.

What was unclear / where operators got stuck
1) Which identity is used by restore job
- Backup job and restore job did not share the same SA/IAM wiring.
- The runbook didn’t call out “confirm restore job serviceAccountName = <expected>” as a precheck.

2) Maintenance mode ordering
- If the runbook says “enter maintenance mode,” it should specify whether it requires API up.
- Today we did: plan -> enable maintenance -> scale down -> destructive action -> restore -> scale up -> validate -> disable maintenance.

3) PITR confidence
- We had no crisp verification step that PITR actually restored to target time.
- We also didn’t know if WAL archiving was configured correctly in this cluster before the drill.

4) Validation output severity
- Need a “red/yellow/green” framing.
- List of critical endpoints and what to do if each fails.

5) Observability gaps
- Dashboards show backups; restores are less visible.
- No step-level progress in restore logs; hard to communicate “what is it doing right now?”

6) Evidence capture
- Olga (Compliance) has asked for a consistent evidence set for customer-facing “DR tested” claims.
- We captured some screenshots but not in a repeatable checklist.

What went well
- Maintenance mode behavior was materially better than last quarter (actionable errors; writes blocked).
- Checksum verification step worked and prevented us from restoring a partial artifact.
- Once permissions were fixed, end-to-end restore flow was mostly coherent (tooling did the heavy lifting).

Action items (to be filed/linked in ENG-4882 unless already tracked)

P0 (before next drill)
- Fix restore job IAM/serviceAccount wiring so it never defaults to “default” SA
  - Owner: Diego Santos
  - Due: 2025-11-22
  - Notes: ensure Helm templates set serviceAccountName for restore job; add chart validation.

- Add explicit pre-flight checklist section to in-place restore runbook
  - Owner: Kira Thompson
  - Due: 2025-11-20
  - Include: confirm backup id, confirm bucket access, confirm restore SA/role, confirm maintenance mode API reachable.

- Add PITR verification query + “what if WAL not configured” branch
  - Owner: Michael Nguyen
  - Due: 2025-11-25
  - Proposed check: select pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp(); and compare to target.

P1 (hardening)
- Improve restore validate output with severity levels and next steps
  - Owner: Ethan Park
  - Due: 2025-12-06
  - Idea: categorize checks: DB connectivity, schema/migrations, API healthz, model catalog, auth.

- Emit structured restore phase metrics/events for dashboards
  - Owner: Sergio Costa
  - Due: 2025-12-10
  - Metric sketch: rw_private_restore_phase{phase="db_restore"}=1, rw_private_restore_duration_seconds, rw_private_restore_success.

- Add “restore annotation” automation on dashboards
  - Owner: Allison Grant
  - Due: 2025-12-10

P2 (docs / customer readiness)
- Create an evidence capture checklist template (screenshots + logs to attach)
  - Owner: Olga Petrov
  - Due: 2025-12-13

- Add a “Common errors” section: AccessDenied, throttling, DB lock contention
  - Owner: Sean Gallagher
  - Due: 2025-12-13

Loose notes / questions to resolve
- Do we want the restore job to run as a distinct “break-glass” role (read-only to backups + limited KMS decrypt) instead of sharing backup role?
- Should maintenance mode be enabled automatically by restore execute (with clear operator prompt) to reduce mistakes?
- Can we produce a single “restore bundle manifest” that includes KMS key id, encryption mode, sizes, checksums, and components included?

Appendix: commands we used (verbatim-ish; redact secrets)
- rw-private-dr backup verify --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z
- rw-private-dr restore plan --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z
- rw-private-dr maintenance enable --reason "DR restore drill"
- kubectl -n redwood-private scale deploy rw-control-plane-api --replicas=0
- kubectl -n redwood-private delete pvc data-rw-postgres-0
- rw-private-dr restore execute --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml --backup-id 2025-11-07T08-00-03Z --mode in-place
- kubectl -n redwood-private rollout status deploy/rw-control-plane-api
- rw-private-dr restore validate --config /etc/redwood/private/config.yaml
- rw-private-dr maintenance disable

Appendix: evidence captured (where)
- Slack thread: incidents/1732639922 has timestamps + AccessDenied snippet.
- Screenshots saved in shared drive folder (same directory) — TODO: consolidate into a single evidence pack for Olga.
